title: CPAT Excel-AI
text:
CPAT Excel-AI


CPAT-AI overview: the mitigation prototypeStatus, user guide, results · PowerPoint, latest version
Use of AI in climate fiscal toolsThe project: Excel-AI, Coded CPAT, other AI tools, timelines · PowerPoint, latest version

Excel-AI is CPAT rebuilt as readable Excel workbooks, generated and checked by AI. The mitigation prototype covers the CPAT mitigation and distribution chain with plain formulas (one formula per block, none over 100 characters), recalculates in about half the time of legacy CPAT, and is checked number for number by independent Python recomputation. Rebuilding it found 228 bugs in legacy CPAT, each fixed in the prototype and written up with a cell-level fix plan; every open modelling question is replicated and tracked.

Chapter 2 is generated from the documents kept beside the code (excel_ai/mitigation/docs/) by make_qmd.py.

title: 1  Overview
text:
1.1 What Excel-AI is
Excel-AI is the Excel side of the CPAT-AI project: Excel prototypes of legacy CPAT, written by Python builders (openpyxl) and checked by LibreOffice recalculation and independent Python recomputation, for modellers and reviewers who work in Excel and for the CPAT team. Its files are in excel_ai/.

title: 1  Overview
text:
Modules. The mitigation prototype (the integrated model, with the distribution tab), the standalone distribution module and the standalone air-pollution module.
Inputs. The policy and parameter inputs are the rows and names of the legacy MTInputs sheet (NameOfParameter), in legacy units. The codes map (docs/CPAT-AI_CodesMap_v<version>.xlsx, tab Inputs) lists every input with its row, its name, its legacy name and its Python key.
Codes and data. Input codes, output codes and the sector and fuel vocabularies are shared with the Python model (the CPAT Python tab), which replicates Excel-AI number for number. Both read the root folder data/ (Section 4.1).
The rule on bugs and issues (Section 1.5).

title: 1  Overview
text:
1.2 Legacy CPAT: the reference
The legacy workbook is the ground truth for both models. The latest version, 1.0pre_465, is kept read-only in data/ (the earlier NoPropData copies of 456, 459 and 465 are no longer in the repository):







File
Role




data/legacy/CPAT 1.0pre_465_Shell.xlsb
The legacy CPAT workbook with its six proprietary tabs empty (every other tab filled); the reference for input rows and names, and for the register’s cell references


data/Public01/legacy/CPAT 1.0pre_465_Public01.xlsb
The shell filled with data edition Public01’s tables (the proprietary ones perturbed)



The legacy workbook is never edited or re-saved; work is done on copies in scratch folders.

title: 1  Overview
text:
1.3 How the work proceeds

Replicate. A block of legacy CPAT is rebuilt in the prototype, formula by formula, with the same sections and the same codes.
Check. An independent Python recomputation of the block reproduces every number; the prototype’s result is compared with legacy’s stored results.
Classify every difference. A difference is either a legacy bug (fixed in the prototype, with a cell-level fix plan for legacy), a legacy issue (replicated and tracked), or a departure decided by the team (tracked).
Release. The builder writes a new version; the quick check, the paste test and the regression against the previous release must pass; the register documents, the tracker, the codes map and the deck are regenerated.
Port. Validated blocks are ported to the Python model (the CPAT Python tab).

title: 1  Overview
text:
1.5 Bugs and issues






ImportantThe rule



Never replicate a legacy bug; always replicate a legacy issue, and track it.


The rule applies to every model of the project, in Excel and in Python. It keeps the prototypes faithful to legacy CPAT where legacy does what it means to, and correct where it does not, and it makes every difference from legacy visible.

1.5.1 Definitions









Kind
Code
Meaning
What the prototype does




Legacy bug
L
Legacy does not compute what it means to: a wrong row, a double application, a dead reference
Fixes it, never replicates it; the fix is written up as a cell-level plan for legacy


Prototype bug
M
A bug found in the prototype itself
Fixes it and records it


Issue
I
Legacy does what it means to, but the choice is open to question
Does the same as legacy and tracks it


Departure
LD
A deliberate difference from legacy that is not a bug fix
Kept only by decision of the team; tracked in the prototype’s LegacyDiff sheet


Upgrade
U
A feature beyond legacy
Tracked



Data problems are issues. They are replicated. Where legacy needs a formula fix to handle the data correctly, that fix is a legacy bug (L) with a cell plan and the issue is ranked Very high; where no cell plan is possible, the prototype aligns with legacy exactly and the issue is ranked Extremely high.

1.5.3 Current counts


231 legacy bugs, 22 prototype bugs, 20 documentation bugs. Legacy 465: 52 fixed (confirmed), 9 fixed with caveats, 2 marked fixed but not fixed, 168 open. (register v1.1.0, excel_ai/core/BUGS.md)
135 issues (14 data problems), 35 departures (LegacyDiff), 14 upgrades. (register v1.1.0, excel_ai/core/ISSUES.md)

The status Legacy 465 records whether the CPAT team has fixed each bug in the latest legacy workbook; each claimed fix is checked against the workbook (excel_ai/bugs_and_legacy/fixes/check465/).


1.5.4 Priorities
Issues and data problems are ranked so the most urgent are seen first: Extremely high and Very high for data problems (as defined above), then Major and Minor. Bugs carry High, Medium or Low by their effect on results.

title: 2  The mitigation prototype
text:
2.1 What it is
Source: excel_ai/mitigation/docs/Documentation.md.
The short guide. Details of every block: the Methods volume. Every legacy bug and issue: the bug-fix register.
The mitigation module of the IMF/World Bank Climate Policy Assessment Tool (CPAT), rebuilt as one readable Excel workbook for one country at a time.
It answers: what do carbon pricing and related policies do to energy prices, energy use, emissions, government revenue and GDP, year by year to 2041?

title: 2  The mitigation prototype
text:
Policies in: carbon tax, a new emissions trading system (ETS) with a cap, feebates, fuel excises, fuel subsidy reform, a methane fee, existing carbon pricing, power-sector policies.
Results out: retail energy prices, fuel use in 16 sectors and 8 fuels, electricity generation and prices, revenue, CO₂ and other greenhouse gases, local air pollutants, GDP effects, the gap to the country’s NDC, and household effects by decile (Distribution tab).
One country, any country: formulas contain no country numbers. Every country value comes from the data tabs, looked up by the country code on Settings (C4). The shipped data are complete for Egypt.
Same as legacy, minus its bugs: it follows legacy CPAT except where legacy has a bug (all fixed) or an open question that we track (issues). See section 5.
Readable and checked: every formula is at most 100 characters and one formula serves a whole block of cells. An independent Python recomputation checks every number.

title: 2  The mitigation prototype
text:
2.2 Quick start

Open CPAT-AI-Mitigation-Prototype_v<version>.xlsm (in excel_ai/; the same file as excel_ai/active_workbooks//CPAT-AI-Mitigation-Prototype_latest.xlsm) in Excel 365 with macros enabled. It opens on ScenarioCompare, the dashboard, without recalculating: the file ships with its values, in manual calculation.
After any change, click Recalculate now (or switch automatic calculation on with Recalculation on/off).
Read the results on ScenarioCompare. Choose Live or Stored results and the year. The key table shows CO₂, GHGs, revenue, the GDP effect and welfare against the baseline; the charts show them over time.
Change a policy on ScenarioDefinition. Column K is the live scenario: for example change CPLevelTarget (carbon price in the target year), then Recalculate now.
Store several scenarios: copy a definition one column to the right, give it a short name (row 2) and Run? = Yes (row 4), then click Run stored scenarios. Results go to StoredOutputs; the dashboard compares up to 10.
Update the data from the data workbook: choose the source on ScenarioCompare, click Update data tables. The status is on Cover.
First time only: click First-run test (grey buttons). The check table must show PASS.

The tabs, left to right: the front (Cover, ScenarioCompare, ScenarioDefinition), the model (Mitigation, Distribution, MTOutputs, StoredOutputs), the inputs (Manual inputs, Settings, Inputs), the data tabs (legacy tables, unchanged), and the reference tabs (version log, differences with legacy, variable dictionary).

title: 2  The mitigation prototype
text:
2.3 How it works
The Mitigation tab runs top to bottom, one section per step, with the section numbers of legacy CPAT. The method of each block, with its equations and pseudocode, is in the website’s CPAT-AI Model tab (https://cpmodelai.github.io/cpat_ai/#model; sources docs/CPAT_model_documentation_qmd/), shared with CPAT Python; the Word Methods volume (docs/methods/) is the compact version. Each scenario is a group of columns: group 1 is the baseline, group 2 the live scenario. Years run across, 2022 to 2041.

2.3.1 Policies (section 1)
Each policy is a path from a start year to a target year, set per scenario on ScenarioDefinition. The carbon price follows that path:
τ(t) = path(t; start year, target year, start level, target level) · (CPI index if the inputs are nominal)
A new ETS starts at a price estimate and is checked against its cap (the goal seek refines it). Feebates act through a shadow price, which changes efficiency but raises no revenue. Existing carbon taxes and ETS prices come from the World Bank Carbon Pricing Dashboard data.
Details: Methods, chapter Prices; chapter ETS.


2.3.2 Energy prices (section 2)
For each fuel and sector, the retail price builds up from the international price:
supply cost  C(t) = fixed part + (C(t−1) − fixed part) · international price(t) / international price(t−1)
retail price R    = (C + excise and other taxes) · (1 + VAT)
after policy P    = R + new carbon tax + ETS price + new excise, each with VAT
Subsidies are negative taxes. Historical prices come from the IMF price data up to the last historical year (2022, as legacy); later years are projected.
Details: Methods, chapter Prices.


2.3.3 Energy demand (sections 5-8, 11)
Fuel use in each sector changes each year with income, its own price and efficiency:
Q(t) = Q(t−1) · (efficiency gain) · (1 + GDP growth)^(income elasticity) · (P(t)/P(t−1))^(price elasticity) · (efficiency response to prices)
The elasticities are legacy CPAT’s. Section 11 adds up fuel use by sector and fuel, including the fuel burnt in power plants.
Details: Methods, appendix A (equations, section 4); chapter Transport for road.


2.3.4 Power (section 3)
Electricity demand comes from the sectors. The power model, as legacy’s engineer model, decides each year:

Dispatch: which plants run, by their variable cost (fuel, carbon price, operation).
Investment: new capacity by technology, chosen by levelised cost with a logit share, within scale-up limits.
Prices: electricity prices from the cost of generation, with taxes, subsidies and price controls.

Power-sector policies (no new coal, nuclear from a year, renewable subsidies, PPAs, rebating revenue, an electricity excise) are set per scenario.
Details: Methods, chapter Power.


2.3.5 Road transport (sections 5, 5b)
By default road fuel use follows the demand elasticities, as every other sector. With TrModel = Engineer, the road engineer model replaces it: vehicle stocks by class, cost of ownership, the choice between combustion and electric vehicles, and vehicle policies (feebates, EV subsidies, purchase taxes, distance tax).
Details: Methods, chapter Transport.


2.3.6 Revenues (section 12)
Revenue is fuel use times the tax per unit, by fuel and sector, for existing taxes, existing subsidies (negative) and new policies:
revenue from new policies = fuel use · (carbon tax + excise + auctioned share · ETS price + VAT on them)
total revenue             = existing taxes + subsidies + new policies + methane fee
The power sector adds its own revenue and subsidies. Feebates are revenue neutral.
Details: Methods, chapter Macro and results.


2.3.7 Emissions (sections 13-15)
CO₂ = fuel use · emission factor        (factors optionally calibrated to the GHG inventory)
Other greenhouse gases (methane, nitrous oxide, F-gases) follow their drivers; methane from fuel supply responds to the methane fee. Local air pollutants (fine particles, sulphur and nitrogen oxides, and others) are fuel use times pollutant factors.
Details: Methods, chapter Emissions.


2.3.8 GDP, carbon pricing indicators, welfare (sections 16-18)
New revenue is fiscal space. How it is used (tax cuts, investment, transfers) moves GDP through fiscal multipliers, one year later:
fiscal space fs(t)  = (new revenue in the scenario − in the baseline) / GDP
GDP effect          = Σ over uses: share of the use · Σ over lags (change in fs · multiplier of the use)
Section 17 reports carbon prices and coverage; section 18 the welfare effects and the gap to the NDC.
Details: Methods, chapter Macro and results.


2.3.9 Distribution (tab Distribution)
Household effects by decile in one analysis year: price changes reach households directly (energy) and indirectly (other goods, through the input-output table); revenue recycling (transfers, targeted by ASPIRE or the poverty line) offsets them.
Details: Methods, chapter Distribution.

title: 2  The mitigation prototype
text:
2.4 Results and the dashboard
ScenarioCompare is the place to read results:

Choices: Live (the scenario groups of Mitigation) or Stored (every stored scenario), and the year.
Key table: energy CO₂, GHGs, revenue, GDP effect and welfare, as levels and differences from the baseline.
Charts: one bar chart of CO₂ and four time-series charts; the title of each is a dropdown of indicators.

MTOutputs lists the key indicators of each live scenario by output code; StoredOutputs keeps the stored scenarios as values. Every row carries a code (for example egy.mit.co2.tot.tot.2: country, module, variable, sector, fuel, scenario), the same codes as the Python model.

title: 2  The mitigation prototype
text:
2.5 Limits and differences from legacy
The rule: never replicate a legacy bug; always replicate a legacy issue, and track it. A bug (L) is legacy computing what it does not intend; the prototype fixes it. An issue (I) is legacy doing what it means to, where the choice is open to question; the prototype does the same. Problems of the input data are issues too (area Data): where legacy reads the data wrongly, the formula fix is a bug with a cell plan and the issue is Very high; where no cell plan is possible, the prototype does exactly what legacy does and the issue is Extremely high (Appendix B). Every item has a code; the codes are explained in Appendix A.

Legacy bugs: the prototype fixes every one, in every module (mitigation, distribution, the inputs). The bugs, with the cell-level fix for legacy CPAT and the status of each in the latest legacy file CPAT 1.0pre_465, are in excel_ai/bugs_and_legacy/Legacy_CPAT_Bugs_v<version>.docx; the master list of bugs and issues is the tracker excel_ai/bugs_and_legacy/Tracking_Legacy_Bugs_v<version>.xlsx.
Issues (data problems first), departures, prototype bugs and upgrades: the appendices below (and the tracker, tab Issues).
Legacy row numbers in the Methods volume are rows of CPAT 1.0pre_456_NoPropData.xlsb, the file the prototype was built and checked against (its data extracts read that file). In CPAT 1.0pre_465 Mitigation rows from 5667 on sit 11 to 15 rows higher. The input sheet ScenarioDefinition has the rows of the 465 MTInputs.
Not built: a few legacy features (upgrades, Appendix E), and the air-pollution co-benefits and transport externalities modules.
Data: the shipped data are Egypt’s; proprietary tables for other countries must be pasted in or linked (issue I90).

title: 2  The mitigation prototype
text:
2.6 Running many scenarios
Source: excel_ai/mitigation/docs/methods/Macro_and_results.md.
Equations: Equations.md; workbook formulas: Formulas.md.
The model calculates two scenarios at a time: the baseline and one live policy scenario. A batch macro copies each scenario definition into the live scenario, calculates it and stores its results as values, which are compared afterwards. This follows legacy CPAT, where a macro copies each scenario column into the column used for calculation and stores the outputs.

2.6.1 Where things are







Place
What it holds




ScenarioDefinition, scenario 1
The baseline, stored once.


ScenarioDefinition, scenario 2
The live policy scenario. The batch run overwrites it with each definition and restores it at the end.


ScenarioDefinition, columns to the right
Scenario definitions, one full ScenarioDefinition column each: short name (row 2, the legend in the charts), Run? (Yes/No), number (previous + 1), name, then the inputs. Red cells differ from the template. To add one, copy the last definition one column to the right and edit it. Blank columns are grouped and collapsed.


Mitigation, Distribution
Two scenario groups: 1 = the baseline (plain formulas), 2 = the live scenario (every calculated cell calls its named LAMBDA). More live scenarios: copy group 2 to the right and set its scenario number; MTOutputs has room for 12 scenario blocks.


MTOutputs
The results of every scenario group in the legacy MTOutputs layout (v1.0.4): columns A Include?, B Country, C Scenario, D CPATIndicator, E CPATCode (our code, from Country, Tab, Variable, SubScenario), F the legacy CPAT code, G Tab, H Variable, I Unit, J SubScenario, years K:AD (distribution rows: deciles 1-10 in K:T); legacy’s sections and rows in legacy order, one block per scenario; a row legacy lists and the prototype does not have stays with Include? = No and the reason (helper columns right of the years: lookups, legacy code body and row, match). Found on Mitigation and Distribution by output code.


StoredOutputs
Results as values only: the MTOutputs indicators of each scenario, under its ID and output code (country.stem.ID). ID 1 is the baseline; a definition keeps its ScenarioDefinition number. Sorted by indicator, then ID (like variables together); every lookup matches the output code, so any order works.


ScenarioCompare
The dashboard and every user entry of the front: results from Live (MTOutputs) or Stored (StoredOutputs), the year, the data source of the linked tables. Core buttons (green) and the others (grey); key results for one year of up to 10 scenarios against the baseline; a bar chart; time series with their chart beside them.


VBA module CPATScenarios
The macros below. The workbook is an .xlsm; the source is also in CPATScenarios.bas.


MacroCheck
Report of the first-run test macro CheckBatchRun.

2.6.3 Main scenario choice and regulations as shadow prices (v0.4.16, LD9)
ScenarioDefinition row 13 (ScenarioSelected, ” - Carbon tax” in every shipped scenario) picks a row of the legacy scenario table (legacy Mitigation rows 222-262, columns N:AC; sheet Mapping, block “Main scenarios”): whether the scenario prices carbon explicitly (legacy row 259), its efficiency adjustment (ScenarioDefinition rows 247-251) and the sectors its shadow price covers (rows 240-257).

Explicit scenarios (carbon tax, total carbon price, coal excise, road fuel tax, electricity emissions tax and excise): the carbon price path of ScenarioDefinition rows 18-21 is the carbon tax (cpx = cptraj), as before.
Shadow-pricing scenarios (feebates, power supply feebates, energy efficiency regulations, power feebate, vehicle fuel economy, residential and industrial efficiency regulations; and “Baseline”): no explicit carbon tax (cpx = 0); the carbon price path becomes a shadow price on the efficiency margin, reg.<sector> = cp.shd x the scenario’s adjustment (energy efficiency 247, vehicle fuel economy 248, residential 249, industrial 250, feebates 251; Egypt 0.7, feebates 1) x 1 if the scenario covers the sector. It enters shpx (with the feebate part, now x row 251, and the ETS benchmark part), so fuel use responds through efficiency only, and power through shk (legacy bugs L87, L88 fixed: legacy’s regulation share is 0 and never reaches power).
The road vehicle feebate of the engineer road model adds reg.rod (the road regulation shadow price) instead of the carbon price, which is in the fuel price already (prototype bug M13).
A text that is not in the table counts as explicit pricing (as the shipped ” - Carbon tax”).



2.6.4 Macros
Core buttons (green, on ScenarioCompare): Recalculate now, Recalculation on/off, Run stored scenarios, Update data tables. The others are grey, below them.

RunAllScenarios (button Run stored scenarios): stores the baseline under ID 1 if none is stored yet. Then, for every definition with Run? = Yes, it copies the definition’s inputs and name into the live scenario (skipping two formula rows), clears the ETS price override and recalculates, runs the ETS goal seek if the definition applies a new ETS without “Override ETS price” = Yes, and stores the live scenario’s outputs as values under the definition’s number and name (replacing that ID’s rows wherever they are). At the end it restores the live scenario, the override and the calculation mode it found, sorts StoredOutputs, groups the blank scenario columns and refreshes the dashboard charts.
RecalculateNow: full recalculation (timed), then the dashboard charts. The workbook ships with its values in manual calculation; ToggleRecalculation switches automatic calculation on or off (for every open workbook, as Excel does).
StoreBaseline: replaces the stored baseline with the current scenario-1 results, after a confirmation.
StoreLiveScenario: stores the live scenario as it stands, under an ID you choose (default: the next free ID from 100).
SolveETSLive: ETS goal seek for the live scenario only. It fills the override prices and switches the override on.
ClearStoredScenarios: deletes every stored scenario except the baseline.
SortStoredOutputs: sorts StoredOutputs by code stem, then ID.
GroupBlankScenarios: groups and collapses the scenario columns of ScenarioDefinition that have no name.
RefreshDashboard: rebuilds the series of the dashboard charts from the scenarios with results in the chosen source (short names in the legend, baseline dashed grey, one colour per scenario slot) and hides the table rows of the others.
CheckBatchRun: the first-run test (section 4). It reruns the batch, so the stored scenarios are recalculated by the application that runs it.

The ETS goal seek is legacy’s damped log-space iteration, as in ets_goalseek.py. It starts from the override prices, or from the fast estimate if there are none. Each step is p × (proposed price / p) ^ alpha, mixed 0.3 with the previous iterate, with 5% smoothing. Alpha halves when the error grows (minimum 0.0625) and rises ×1.2 when the error more than halves (maximum 1). It stops when the worst |covered / cap − 1| is below 0.5%, or after 20 iterations.


2.6.5 First run in Excel
The VBA project (written by vba_project.py) and the stored results were produced without Excel. They are tested in LibreOffice: the module loads, the macros reproduce the Python emulation, and CheckBatchRun passes. To confirm the same in Excel:

If the file was downloaded, unblock it first (file Properties > Unblock), or Excel opens it with macros disabled.
Open it and choose Enable Content.
Run CheckBatchRun (Alt+F8); it takes a minute or two. It checks the 12 lookups the macros rely on (sheets, rows by code, scenario columns, MTOutputs blocks); compares Excel’s own recalculation of the baseline with the stored baseline (plain formulas only, so Excel and LibreOffice calculate it the same way); and reruns RunAllScenarios, ETS goal seek included, comparing every stored value with the value stored before.
MacroCheck shows Result PASS when no value differs by more than 1e-6 (relative). CHECK lists how many values differ; FAIL names the lookup that was not found.
If Excel cannot load the VBA project, or Alt+F8 lists no macros: remove the project if one is listed, import CPATScenarios.bas (Alt+F11 > File > Import), save as .xlsm and run CheckBatchRun again.



2.6.6 Comparing and keeping results

Source and year. On ScenarioCompare choose Results from (Stored or Live) and the year, then Recalculate now. Stored reads StoredOutputs (every stored scenario); Live reads MTOutputs (the scenario groups of Mitigation: the baseline and the live scenario, and any group added by copy-paste). The names SCVal, SCCode and SCYear choose the range with CHOOSE; every value is INDEX(SCVal, MATCH(country.stem.ID, SCCode, 0), year column), so the order of the rows never matters.
Scenario slots. Up to 10, in ScenarioDefinition order: ID, short name (the legend), name. A scenario with no result in the chosen source shows blank (key table) or #N/A (time series, hidden by a conditional format, a gap in the charts); the charts leave it out.
Key table. Energy CO2 emissions, GHG emissions excluding LULUCF, revenue as a share of GDP, the GDP effect of the revenue use and the net welfare effect: level, difference from the baseline, and % difference for the two emission levels. The bar chart beside it shows the % difference of energy CO2 by scenario.
Time series. Four tables (default: energy CO2, GHGs, revenue, GDP effect), scenarios down and years across, each with its line chart beside it. The title of each table is a dropdown of the indicator list at the bottom of the tab: every MTOutputs indicator except the price and Kaya indices.
StoredOutputs holds values only, so results from other files can be pasted in as values under new IDs, as long as its column layout is kept (output code in column D).
The baseline changes only when StoreBaseline is run.



2.6.7 Limits

The batch run calculates one policy scenario at a time. Further Mitigation scenario groups (copies of group 2) show on the dashboard under Live; the batch macros use the live scenario (group 2) only.
MTOutputs (the legacy MTOutputs rows the prototype has and its own key outputs) defines what is stored: its Mitigation rows, each code once (about 830 per scenario); the distribution rows are live only. To store more, add rows to the MTOutputs blocks first.

title: 2  The mitigation prototype
text:
2.7 The data tabs
Source: excel_ai/mitigation/docs/methods/Data_tabs.md.
User request (2026-10-17): align the data tabs with legacy CPAT (grouped by module, legacy order, legacy names and content where possible, without undoing principled decisions); check that the model would work with the full all-country data; put every Egypt-only table alone on its tab or at the bottom; check how far the legacy data tables can be copied in. Then (same day): align more fully, going with the recommendations. The norm is NORMS.md 1.5.

2.7.1 Summary

Order. The data tabs sit under the legacy dividers in legacy order: DATA_MITIGATION->>, DATA_DISTN->>, DATA_TRAN->>, DATA_OUTPUT->>; tabs without a legacy data tab come last under DATA_OTHER->> (BaselineCO2 only).
Copy-in rules (NORMS 1.5).

L, a single legacy table: the table itself, unchanged (same columns, column letters and codes; header row 3, data from A4; a key formula column right of the table where legacy has no unique key). Paste the legacy data rows at A4. 17 tabs: Balances, EnergyCons, CH4Inputs, UNPop, OilProductShares (v0.4.12), WEO, EF_GHG, SCC, EF_PM, IO_GTAP, HHSurvey, HH_Elast, ASPIRE, WHOCooking, GDPRatios, Transport1, Transport2.
A, a legacy tab with several tables: kept at its legacy cell addresses from row 3 (rows 1-2: source line and title bar). Paste the legacy tab from row 3. 10 tabs: Countries, Elasticities, ETS+LTS, Multipliers, Prices_int, ECP, Transport3 (stored results, rows 5+) and, since v0.4.7, Power, CoC and GHGs (the inventory and, rows 1201-1388, the 2023-2024 emission shocks of the power model).
**L*, Prices_dom:** legacy header rows and codes; paste legacy rows 4 onwards at A1.

Country selection is a data step (NORMS 1.5, rule 2c). What legacy Mitigation computes from these tabs for the selected country sits in blocks of the Inputs tab, by formula, under the keys the model already used:

Inputs_ela: elasticities (the country’s column of Elasticities, as legacy column G);
Inputs_mult: multipliers (median ± standard deviation by group, instrument and lag);
Inputs_macro: GDP growth and levels, deflators, exchange rate (WEO series with legacy’s extension past the last data year, rows 417-467) and the energy trade balance and share traded (rows 741-743, from Balances);
Inputs_pint: international price series by source (rows 633-695);
Inputs_ecp: existing carbon pricing (rows 1675-1764; v0.4.12: carbon tax with single and fuel rates, national ETS and EU ETS, each code looked up in its own legacy block of ECP, coverage by data year, and two tables by ECP sector and fuel: carbon tax and ETS in $/tCO2);
Inputs_ef: CO2 emission factors (rows 980-1011);
Inputs_nc (v0.9.0): non-CO2 combustion emission factors of local pollutants and CH4 by legacy EF code (rows 1052-1663: country, else World Bank region, else world, from the all-country EF_PM; other energy the maximum across the other subsectors);
v0.4.7, power (legacy section 4, rows 2954-4300): Inputs_pset (the power settings of ScenarioDefinition scenario 1 and derived values, each a defined name Ps…), Inputs_ptech (one row per generation type, the former PowerTech: country, else world parameters, efficiency and generation from Balances, WACC from CoC, capacity factors), Inputs_ppath (year paths, the former PowerPaths: capex time factors, storage, income factor, fuel price shocks, prices) and Inputs_ppar (parameters, the former PowerParams). The chains are mapped in chapter Power. The Egypt values reproduce legacy’s cached values (macro series to 1e-15; power data to 1e-12), apart from one legacy bug fixed (L51: the coal trade balance was valued at the oil price) and one stale value in legacy’s stored run (I38: the wind and solar capex time factors for 2039-2041 differ from the legacy Power cells they reference; the prototype follows the Power tab).

Proprietary tables. The public legacy file (CPAT 1.0pre_456_NoPropData.xlsb) holds Egypt only in Balances, EnergyCons (empty), Prices_dom, EF_PM, IO_GTAP, HHSurvey, ASPIRE, WHOCooking, CalVal and Tran_Scatter. The model uses the first eight; all eight paste in directly.
All-country test: PASS. check_allcountry.py clones every Egypt row of every single-table tab under a dummy country (XEG) at the bottom of its table, renames Egypt’s codes to XEG in place on the tabs kept at legacy addresses, selects XEG and recalculates: no error values, every output of Mitigation and Distribution identical to Egypt’s.
No table from legacy’s cached Egypt run is left (v0.4.7). The former PowerTech, PowerPaths and PowerParams are computed from the legacy tabs on Inputs. BaselineCO2 (the scenario-1 CO2 the calibration uses) is derived by the build.
Legacy bugs in the power data: all fixed (v0.4.10, NORMS 0; v0.4.7 still copied them): L52 every generation type takes the country parameters where they exist (Egypt: solar fixed O&M 11.831 instead of 15 $/kW/y); L53 the actual capacity factor of the base year (installed capacity, Power rows 358-1635) is used inside the CFOverride bounds (Egypt: gas 0.385, wind 0.436, solar 0.347, hydro 0.592; base-year gas capacity 52 GW instead of 35); L54 hydro invests from the base year only when its generation share is above 50% (Egypt: from 2030); L55 the country rows are looked up in the country block first (China, Japan, Korea); L56 countries without CoC risk data take the default WACC, flagged.
Balances, EnergyCons, EF_PM, IO_GTAP, HHSurvey, HH_Elast, ASPIRE, WHOCooking and GDPRatios became legacy tables (v0.4.5). Then GHGs, CH4Inputs, UNPop, EF_GHG, SCC, Transport1 and Transport2 followed. The tables come from extract_legacy_tables.py, which writes legacy_<Tab>.csv verbatim from the legacy file (today into the legacy-form cache .buildcache/legacy_csv/<edition>/, saved to data/<edition>/tidy/ by data/scripts/legacy_csv.py).
Base-year fuel use and power demand now come from Balances through legacy’s flow mapping (Mapping columns J-M), as legacy does with BalancesOrConsumption = Balances; the old PowerDemand tab was dropped.
CO2 emission factors: the legacy EF_GHG table replaces the Egypt factors copied from legacy’s run. The selection of legacy Mitigation rows 980-1011 is now a data step on Inputs, and it reproduces the Egypt factors exactly:

the country’s code, else its World Bank region, else the world;
LPG and kerosene in power, and coal, LPG, kerosene and other oil products in road, take the row legacy points to;
jet fuel uses the IEA factor (EFJetIEA);
biomass is zero.

GHGs: the legacy table adds Zimbabwe 2021 (legacy row 947). The previous extract stopped at row 946.
All named ranges over data tables reach the capacity of the full legacy tables, with margin.
v0.4.6: Countries, Elasticities, ETS+LTS, Multipliers, Prices_int, ECP and Transport3 became legacy tabs at legacy addresses (legacy_<Tab>_cells.csv in the legacy-form cache), WEO the legacy table; the selections legacy makes for the country became the Inputs blocks above; the GHG inventory year and every other lookup are unchanged.
v0.4.6 results against v0.4.5: unchanged except the coal trade balance (L51 fixed; external balance rows xtb, about 0.6 bn USD a year for Egypt) and the base-year lagged GDP growth of the road model (trgdl, 2022: the WEO 2021 growth 3.25 % instead of 0, transport bug B2 now fixed, as the builder intended; the old WEO copy had no 2021 growth).
v0.4.7: Power, CoC and GHGs became legacy tabs at legacy addresses; the power data of the country (the former tabs PowerTech, PowerPaths and PowerParams, copied from legacy’s Egypt run) became the Inputs power blocks, formulas only (country, else world parameters; efficiency and generation from Balances; WACC from CoC; capex time factors, storage, income factor, emission shocks; settings from ScenarioDefinition scenario 1). The values reproduce the former tables, except the wind and solar capex time factors for 2039-2041 (I94). Effect on Egypt’s results: none before 2039; from 2039 new capacity and investment of solar, wind and gas, then power fuel use and emissions (525 output codes; largest: new solar investment in the baseline, by up to 149 MW a year).
Dropped in v0.4.7: PowerTech, PowerPaths, PowerParams (now Inputs blocks from Power, CoC, Balances, WEO, GHGs).
v0.4.12: OilProductShares (legacy table, all countries; household share of diesel, kerosene, LPG and gasoline, and their road shares) after UNPop, as legacy. Inputs_prices multiplies the VAT rate of gasoline, diesel, LPG and kerosene by the household share, as legacy rows 797-816 (LD5, issue I39). Settings rows 46-51: the methane fee switches per source of legacy Manual inputs J196-J200 (LD46; since v0.5.2 on sheet Manual inputs, shown on Settings). Inputs columns efxs:eff (v0.9.0: removed, legacy 465 factors; nearest GAINS factors, bug L59) and ecpk, xcp0 (existing carbon pricing), which replace ctc and etc.



2.7.2 Manual inputs: the second input source, at the legacy addresses
Sheet Manual inputs (tab group INPUTS->>, after ScenarioDefinition) is the whole legacy tab of that name, rows 3-378 at their legacy cell addresses (rows 1-2: source line and title bar), so the legacy tab pasted from row 3 replaces it. title: 3  Other modules
text:
3.1 Distribution module
The mitigation prototype is the integrated model. Two further modules are standalone workbooks that take their inputs from it: the distribution module and the air-pollution module. Every module is published under <Name>_latest in excel_ai/active_workbooks/, through which the modules link to each other.
The standalone distribution module (excel_ai/CPAT-AI-Distribution-Prototype_v<version>.xlsm) computes the household effects by decile of a mitigation scenario: price changes, budget shares, direct and indirect effects, revenue recycling and welfare. Its method is the Distribution tab of the mitigation prototype, explained in the CPAT-AI Model tab (Distribution).
One copy of the formulas. The module is cut from the built mitigation prototype: its Distribution and FromMitigation tabs, the distribution data tabs, ScenarioDefinition (distribution rows shown) and Settings. To change a formula, change the mitigation builder, rebuild the prototype, then rebuild the module.
One input tab. Its only input from Mitigation is the tab FromMitigation: the values of the prototype’s export block (section 19a, defined name ExportDistn), in the Mitigation column layout. The button Update from Mitigation on Cover copies those values from the mitigation workbook named on Cover. If that workbook is open, its current values are used; otherwise it is opened read-only, without macros or recalculation. The module runs one scenario at a time.
Build and check.
The check confirms that the Distribution tab equals the prototype’s cell for cell, that FromMitigation equals section 19a through the macro’s row mapping, that no formula reads a dropped tab or an undefined name, and, end to end, that a carbon price changed in the prototype and carried over by the update gives the same Distribution.

title: 3  Other modules
text:
cd excel_ai/distribution
python build_distribution.py    # the module, about 1 minute
python check_distribution.py    # about 4 minutes

title: 3  Other modules
text:
3.2 Air-pollution module
The air-pollution module (excel_ai/air_pollution/) is a standalone rebuild of the Air Pollution module of legacy CPAT 1.0pre_459. It starts from the pollutant emissions produced by Mitigation and does not recalculate fuel use or emissions.
Boundary. The inputs are the baseline and policy emission series keyed by the codes aps.<pollutant>.<sector>, with year, country, unit, scenario and source traceability. In legacy 459 the handoff is country.mit.em.<pollutant>.<sector>.<scenario> in tonnes per year; the current Mitigation outputs are in kt, so units are converted explicitly at the boundary. Once the input block is filled, the workbook runs without links to another workbook.
Scope. The module reproduces the calculations and options of legacy 459: emissions to concentrations, exposure and health burden, and economic outputs, for baseline and policy scenarios and their difference. Fuel externalities are reported as outputs only and are not fed back into Mitigation prices.
Status. The current workbook holds the scaffold: Cover, Data Sources, Mitigation Inputs and the nine public reference tables extracted from legacy 459 (the ap459_* tables of data/Public01/tidy/). The calculations, unit conversion, outputs and the numerical regression are open. The first regression case is Senegal, the country selected in the legacy NoPropData dashboard.
Validation. Each selected output is compared with legacy 459 by scenario and year, and every difference is classified as a confirmed bug fix, a replicated issue, or unresolved. Numerical equivalence is not claimed until the selected country has populated, reproducible inputs.

title: 3  Other modules
text:
3.3 Road transport co-benefits
The prototype reads the road-transport co-benefits as values typed on its tab FromTransportCB, as it reads the air-pollution marginal damages on FromAirPollution (both 0 for countries without values). They feed the Pigouvian components of the prototype. A standalone transport co-benefits module is planned to supply them.

title: 4  Data and working practice
text:
4.1 Data
The data the models read, the norms the project works under, and where everything is in the repository.
All data of the project live in the root folder data/ (rebuilt 2026-10-30). The tidy tables are the source of truth; the legacy-compatible workbook is written from them. Code reads the data from there by a path relative to the repository; nothing is copied into the project folders.

title: 4  Data and working practice
text:
4.2 Working in the repository
The project works under written norms (excel_ai/core/NORMS.md). They bind people and AI agents alike; AGENTS.md at the root of the repository routes any AI agent to them. This section summarises the norms that shape the files a reader meets; NORMS.md is the authority.

4.2.1 Files, versions and releases
Where the files are. People open the workbooks in excel_ai/active_workbooks/ (<Name>_latest, the permalinked copies the modules link to). Every version of a module workbook, the current one included, is in the module’s releases/ folder as <Name>_v<version>.<ext> (for example excel_ai/mitigation/releases/CPAT-AI-Mitigation-Prototype_v1.1.0.xlsm). The documents:








File
Where
What it is

The legacy bugs, with every cell-level fix plan

BUGS.md, ISSUES.md, NORMS.md, TODO.md, CAVEATS.md
excel_ai/core/
The bug and issue lists, the rules, the open work, the task log




Older versions of the documents move to excel_ai/bugs_and_legacy/register/releases/ (the deck’s to excel_ai/mitigation/releases/) when a new version is written (excel_ai/core/tools/release.py).
Version numbers. Three parts, 0.<major>.<minor>, until the first full release 1.0.0: the last part for fixes and small features, the middle part for structural or methodological change. Each module with its own builder (distribution, air pollution) has its own version and records which mitigation version it was built from. Files released before the change to three parts were renamed; their contents keep the old two-part numbers. The register documents, the tracker and the codes map carry the version of the mitigation prototype they were made with.
One version table per workbook and generated document, in the same columns: version, date, description (with register codes), and the largest regression difference against the previous release.



4.2.2 Checks








Check
When
What it does




Quick check (check_quick.py)
After every change; a few minutes
Structure, names, literals, formula length, a full recalculation with no error cells, the code protocol, the change of every output code against the last release


Paste test (check_paste.py)
Every release
Pastes the live scenario’s column group into further groups, as a user would, and checks that the pasted groups number themselves, show no errors and reproduce the stored results


Full check (check_full.py)
At a milestone; several hours
Everything, including the macro tests


Independent recomputation
Within the checks
Python reference models of the power, transport and distribution blocks reproduce the workbook’s numbers



Every increment is a regression test: the new version’s values are compared with the previous release, and every difference is zero or explained in the version table.


4.2.3 Excel written by code
The Excel prototypes are written with openpyxl and recalculated in LibreOffice, so they build and check on Linux and in cloud sessions. Excel 365 is used for review only. The norms set the column layout of every sheet type, a visual style guide (colours, fonts, borders, sections), formula rules (at most 100 characters; one formula serves a whole block), copy-paste ability of scenario columns, and lint rules that every file passes before it ships so Excel never shows a repair prompt.


4.2.4 Task completion
Every finished task ends with an entry at the bottom of excel_ai/core/CAVEATS.md, the single record of completed work: the task, its inputs, its outputs and its caveats. Earlier entries may be corrected but not deleted. Open work is listed in excel_ai/core/TODO.md and coded/TODO.md.
Norms follow the lessons. A mistake whose cause could recur ends with a norm and a check that would have caught it, added in the same task.


4.2.5 Methodology and version notes
A methodology describes the method as it is now, for a reader who has never seen an earlier version. Change history goes in separate version notes: the version tables and CAVEATS.md.
